analysis.one_liner: Lets striking workers collect unemployment benefits after two weeks on strike.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than a Senate committee: introduced with four Senate backers, it has had no hearing, vote, or action since it was referred to the Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal rules, states may not pay unemployment benefits to workers who are off the job because of a labor dispute. This bill would change that: once a strike lasts two weeks, workers would be eligible for unemployment benefits as if they were unemployed, and benefits would start immediately for workers locked out by their employer or permanently replaced. It would also waive the usual requirement that claimants be available for work, since striking workers are still employed. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Striking workers and workers idled as an indirect result of a labor dispute, who would get a paycheck substitute after two weeks on strike or immediately if locked out or permanently replaced. Unions gain leverage, because members can hold out longer without losing all income.

how_it_helps.text: Workers on strike would be treated as if unemployed and paid benefits beginning 14 days after a strike begins, instead of receiving nothing for the duration of the dispute [S2].
Benefits would begin immediately on the date a lock-out began, the date an employer hired permanent replacement workers, or the date the dispute ended and the worker became unemployed [S2].
Workers idled as an indirect result of a labor dispute, such as supplier or customer employees caught in someone else's strike, would also qualify [S2].
The bill exempts these claimants from the work-availability requirement in the Social Security Act, so they are not disqualified for being attached to their own job [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who fund unemployment insurance through payroll taxes and can face higher tax rates when their former employees draw benefits, and the state-federal unemployment insurance system, which would bear new payouts during strikes.

drawbacks.text: Unemployment insurance is funded by employer payroll taxes, so paying benefits during strikes would raise costs for employers and potentially for the state-federal UI system [S2].

A standard objection to this policy is that guaranteed strike income may encourage longer or more frequent strikes, prolonging disputes and adding to benefit outlays; the bill contains no offsetting revenue or cost control [S2].

The bill imposes a new federal mandate on state unemployment programs, which administer benefits and would have to conform their laws, an obligation states have historically resisted when Congress has expanded eligibility [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers caught in long strikes or lockouts, the benefit is substantial: a safety net where there is currently none, and it removes the employer tactic of waiting out strikers or hiring permanent replacements. The main cost is real but narrower: higher unemployment insurance outlays and employer taxes concentrated in periods of labor conflict, and a risk of longer disputes. The design is straightforward, though it provides no dedicated funding for the new payouts.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it sits there with no path to a vote yet.

narrative.text: Sen. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on September 8, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S4].
No further action has been recorded since the referral: no hearings, markup, or floor vote appear in the action history [S4].
Four senators cosponsored the bill: three of the 45 Senate Democrats and one of the two independents; no Republicans signed on [S3].
The bill changes federal unemployment insurance rules, which fall under the jurisdiction of the Finance Committee, so that committee's action is the necessary next step [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would bear the cost of strike benefits are better off so far, because the bill has not advanced and no worker has gained eligibility; striking workers have gained nothing yet.

for.name: Sen. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was read twice and referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action: no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters are Democrats or independents, with no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee has not acted on it.

industries.note: Unions gain bargaining leverage because members can sustain a strike after two weeks without losing all income; the workers themselves get a benefit where the law currently allows none.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those facing strikes and lockouts
industries.note: Employers fund unemployment insurance through payroll taxes and would face higher payouts and tax rates when their workers strike, weakening their ability to wait out or replace strikers.
States would gain a federal mandate to pay a new class of claims but bear the administrative burden and outlays, which flow to their workers.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a 55-seat Republican Senate majority, and no action in the Finance Committee since referral, the bill is very likely to die in committee without a vote, as most labor-related bills introduced by minority-party senators do. Its best realistic path is inclusion as a provision in a broader bill, which is uncommon for unemployment insurance expansions.
